body:
Valleys and ridges

A valley is an elongated low area between higher land surfaces. A river or stream commonly flows through its lowest part.

A ridge is an elongated area of elevated land. A spur is a projecting extension of higher land that extends from a hill or ridge into lower terrain.

Valleys and spurs can both produce V-shaped bends in contour lines. Their distinction depends on the direction in which the pointed ends of the contour bends face relative to higher and lower ground.

Contour pattern of a river valley

When a contour crosses a stream valley, it generally bends into a V shape. The pointed end of the V faces towards higher ground and upstream.

Water flows downhill towards lower elevation. Its direction of flow is therefore opposite to the direction in which the pointed end of the V faces.

For example, suppose a river crosses contours of 160 m, 140 m, 120 m and 100 m from north to south. The river flows southwards, and the V-shaped contour bends point northwards, towards higher elevation.

In a normal river valley, the contour V points upstream, while the river flows downstream in the opposite direction.

Contour pattern of a spur

A spur projects from higher ground towards lower ground. Its contours also bend into a V or U shape, but the pointed or projecting end faces downhill, towards lower elevations.

Suppose the contour elevations decrease from 160 m in the north to 100 m in the south. A southward-projecting spur will have contour bends whose pointed ends face southwards.

FeatureDirection of contour bend
ValleyTowards higher ground
SpurTowards lower ground

The terms V-shaped valley and V-shaped contour bend describe different aspects of terrain. A V-shaped valley refers to the cross-sectional shape of a valley, whereas the contour V refers to the shape of contour lines viewed from above.

V-shaped valleys, U-shaped valleys and gorges

V-shaped valley

A V-shaped valley has a narrow floor and sides that rise away from the river. It commonly develops through river erosion, particularly where downward erosion is significant.

U-shaped valley

A U-shaped valley typically has a comparatively broad floor and steep sides. Such valleys commonly develop through glacial erosion.

Gorge

A gorge is a deep, narrow valley with very steep sides. Its contour lines are closely spaced along the valley sides.

Saddle and watershed

A saddle is a relatively low area between 2 higher summits. On a contour map, the surrounding elevated land may produce a pinched contour pattern between the summits.

A watershed or drainage divide is elevated ground separating adjacent drainage basins. Water on opposite sides of the divide generally flows towards different drainage systems.

Ridges frequently act as drainage divides. Valleys, in contrast, commonly collect surface runoff.

Determining the direction of river flow

The direction of flow can be identified by examining labelled contour elevations, contour bends where a river crosses them, and any flow-direction arrows shown on the map.

A river flowing from the 200 m contour towards the 100 m contour is moving from higher to lower ground. Its geographical direction depends on the map's orientation.

A river does not necessarily flow southward simply because it appears to flow down the printed page. North, south, east and west must be determined from the north arrow or geographical coordinates.

Prelims focus

  • The contour V in a river valley normally points upstream.
  • The projecting end of a spur points towards lower ground.
  • River flow follows decreasing elevation under normal conditions.
  • Gorges have narrow valleys and steep sides.
  • Ridges frequently separate drainage basins.
  • Trap: The V-shaped contour bend of a valley must not be confused with the downhill-pointing bend of a spur.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 5, Topographical Maps, pp. 57-60; Arizona State University, Topographic and Geologic Maps, Figure 4-3, p. 3, consulted 26 November 2026; University of Saskatchewan, Introductory Physical Geology Laboratory Manual, Chapter 7, Topographic Maps, section on the Rule of Vs for Contour Lines, pp. 7-10, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Valleys, Ridges, Spurs and River Flow on Contour Maps

body:
Purpose of thematic mapping

A thematic map represents the spatial distribution or geographical variation of a selected subject. Unlike a general-purpose map, it concentrates on particular information, such as annual rainfall, population density, soil types or crop production.

Thematic maps help reveal geographical patterns, concentrations and regional differences that may be difficult to recognise from statistical tables alone.

Qualitative and quantitative thematic maps

A qualitative thematic map represents different categories or types of geographical features. Examples include soil-type maps, geological maps showing rock categories and maps showing different types of vegetation.

A quantitative thematic map represents numerical quantities or variations. Examples include maps of population density, annual rainfall and agricultural production.

Dot maps

A dot distribution map uses dots of equal size, each representing a specified quantity. It is useful for displaying the distribution of population, livestock, agricultural production or similar countable phenomena.

For example, if 1 dot represents 1,000 people, an area containing 8 dots represents 8,000 people. An area containing 3 dots represents 3,000 people.

The placement of dots should reflect the known geographical distribution of the phenomenon. However, a dot does not necessarily identify the precise location of each individual represented by it.

Choropleth maps

A choropleth map uses different colours, shades or patterns to represent values associated with predefined geographical areas, such as states, districts or countries.

Choropleth maps are particularly suitable for comparing rates, ratios, percentages and densities. Population density and literacy rate are common examples.

Consider 2 imaginary districts:

  • District A has 8,000 people and an area of 20 km2. Its population density is 400 people per km2.
  • District B has 3,000 people and an area of 5 km2. Its population density is 600 people per km2.

District A has the larger total population, but District B has the greater population density. A choropleth map showing density would assign District B to a higher density category only if the legend places the 2 densities in different ranges.

Using unadjusted population totals to compare areas of very different sizes can produce a misleading impression of population concentration.

Isopleth maps

An isopleth map uses lines connecting places having the same value of a geographical variable. Such lines are collectively known as isolines.

Unlike choropleth shading, isolines can extend across administrative boundaries. They are useful for variables that change continuously over geographical space, such as temperature, rainfall and atmospheric pressure.

IsolineEqual quantity represented
Contour or isohypseElevation
IsothermTemperature
IsobarAtmospheric pressure
IsohyetRainfall
IsobathWater depth

For example, an isohyet marked 800 mm joins locations receiving 800 mm of rainfall during the period specified by the map. It does not necessarily follow district or state boundaries.

Proportional symbol and flow maps

A proportional symbol map uses symbols whose size varies according to the quantity represented. For example, larger circles may represent cities with larger populations.

A flow map represents the movement of people, goods, water or other phenomena between places. Lines or arrows indicate connections or movement, and their width may represent the quantity of movement.

Unlike a proportional symbol map, a dot density map normally uses dots of the same size and varies their number to represent different quantities.

Choosing the appropriate representation

Geographical informationSuitable method
Distribution of livestock numbersDot map
District-wise population densityChoropleth map
Continuous rainfall variationIsopleth map
Relative population sizes of citiesProportional symbol map
Movement of goods between placesFlow map

Interpreting thematic information correctly

Before comparing thematic values, examine the variable being represented, its measurement unit, the geographical area, the data period and the legend.

For example, a rainfall map may show annual rainfall or rainfall during a particular month. These maps cannot be compared correctly without considering their time periods.

Maps showing categories, such as soil types, do not necessarily use darker colours to indicate greater quantities. The colours may simply distinguish different categories.

Prelims focus

  • Dot maps use equal-sized dots representing fixed quantities.
  • Choropleth maps commonly represent area-based densities, rates and percentages.
  • Isopleth maps represent equal values using lines.
  • Isotherms join equal temperatures; isohyets join equal rainfall values.
  • Isobars join equal atmospheric pressure values.
  • Trap: The region with the largest population need not have the highest population density.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 1, Types of Maps Based on Function, pp. 8-13; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part II, Class 12, Chapter 3, Graphical Representation of Data, sections on Thematic Maps, Dot Maps, Choropleth Maps, Isopleth Maps and Flow Maps, accessed through IIT Kanpur's SATHEE textbook resource, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Thematic Maps and the Representation of Geographical Data

body:
Why map projections are necessary

The Earth is approximately spherical, although slightly flattened near the poles. Its curved surface cannot be transferred perfectly onto a flat sheet without introducing some distortion.

This can be understood by imagining the peel of an orange. When the curved peel is flattened, it must stretch, tear, overlap or change its shape.

A map projection is a systematic method of transferring locations and the network of latitudes and longitudes from the curved surface of the Earth onto a flat surface.

A projection allows the geographical positions of features to be represented on a flat map. Different projections distribute distortion differently according to their intended purposes.

Properties affected by projection

The principal geographical properties that map projections attempt to preserve are:

  • Area: The relative sizes of geographical regions.
  • Shape: The form of features, particularly over small areas.
  • Distance: The separation between geographical locations.
  • Direction: The orientation of one location relative to another.

No flat world map can preserve all 4 properties everywhere simultaneously. A projection may preserve one property accurately while introducing distortion in others.

Projections classified by their basic form

Cylindrical projections

A cylindrical projection can be understood through the model of a cylinder surrounding the globe. The geographical network is transferred to the cylindrical surface, which can then be opened into a flat map.

In a normal cylindrical projection, the meridians are commonly represented by parallel straight lines and the parallels by straight lines crossing them.

Cylindrical projections are widely used for world maps, although their properties vary depending on the particular projection.

Conical projections

A conical projection can be understood through the model of a cone placed around the globe. In its normal form, meridians appear as lines converging towards a common point, while parallels appear as circular arcs.

Conical projections are often suitable for regions in middle latitudes with a substantial east-west extent.

Azimuthal or planar projections

A planar projection uses a plane as its conceptual projecting surface. When centred on a pole, it provides a convenient representation of the surrounding polar region.

Azimuthal projections preserve directions from their designated centre, although distances, areas or shapes may be distorted elsewhere.

The cylinder, cone and plane are useful conceptual models. Not all modern projections are produced through literal optical projection; many are defined mathematically.

Projections classified by preserved properties

Projection typeMain property preservedImportant limitation
Equal-areaRelative areasShapes may be distorted
ConformalLocal angles and shapesAreas may be distorted
EquidistantDistances from selected points or along selected linesNot all distances are correct
AzimuthalDirections from a selected centreDirections between arbitrary points need not be correct

Equal-area projections are also called homolographic projections. Conformal projections are also called orthomorphic projections.

Some projections adopt a compromise approach, reducing several types of distortion without perfectly preserving any single property throughout the map.

Mercator projection

The Mercator projection was introduced by Gerardus Mercator in 1569. It is a conformal cylindrical projection.

In its normal form, the meridians are equally spaced vertical lines, while the parallels are horizontal lines whose spacing increases towards the poles.

The Mercator projection preserves local angles and represents routes of constant compass bearing as straight lines. A route of constant bearing is called a rhumb line. These characteristics made the projection particularly useful for navigation.

However, the projection greatly exaggerates the size of geographical regions at high latitudes. The North Pole and South Pole cannot be represented at finite positions on the ordinary Mercator projection.

Consequently, a high-latitude region may appear much larger relative to an equatorial region than it actually is. The Mercator projection is therefore unsuitable for accurate visual comparison of the relative areas of continents and countries.

Choosing a projection according to purpose

  • For comparing the relative areas of geographical regions, an equal-area projection is appropriate.
  • For representing constant-bearing navigation routes, the Mercator projection has an important advantage.
  • For examining polar regions, a suitably centred planar projection can be useful.
  • For a middle-latitude region extending mainly east-west, an appropriate conical projection may be suitable.

Projection choice depends on both geographical extent and the property that must be preserved. Distortion is generally easier to control when mapping a small region than when representing the entire Earth.

Prelims focus

  • Every flat world map introduces some geographical distortion.
  • Equal-area projections preserve relative areas.
  • Conformal projections preserve local angles and shapes.
  • Azimuthal projections preserve directions from their centre.
  • Mercator is a conformal cylindrical projection with increasing distortion towards the poles.
  • Trap: An equidistant projection does not preserve every distance between every pair of points.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Map Projections, pp. 35-46; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 15, p. 114, consulted 26 November 2026; U.S. Geological Survey, How Are Different Map Projections Used?, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Map Projections and Geographical Distortion
